text: Lipschitz stability for identification of piecewise constant conductivity in parabolic equation from finitely many interior point measurements The difference between two piecewise constant functions is bounded by a constant times the difference between their Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps. This bound holds in the infinity norm for the functions and in the operator norm for the maps. The conductivity is uniquely determined by its Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. The relationship is Lipschitz continuous. The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. The reconstruction of the current is Lipschitz stable. The difference between two reconstructed currents is bounded by a constant times the difference between their corresponding internal functionals. The constant depends on given parameters and bounds. This ensures that small changes in the input lead to controlled changes in the output. Under certain smoothness conditions on the domain and boundary data, if two functions are bounded and Lipschitz, equal on the boundary, and share the same potential, then their difference in the interior is controlled by the difference of their corresponding solutions. The estimate involves a constant exponent and a multiplicative constant depending on various parameters. The bound is expressed in terms of Holder-type norms. This result provides stability for an inverse problem or parameter identification.

title: Theorem 1.3 — Conditional Stability for Single Interior Measurement
text: The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. {\rm (Main Theorem)} {\it Let $d > 0$ and $\Omega _d := \{ x \in \Omega \, :\,  \operatorname {dist}(x,\,  \mathbb {R}^n \setminus \Omega ) > d\} $. Let $\gamma _1, \gamma _2$ be an admissible pair and $A, \rho , \gamma _1, \gamma _2, \omega ^2$ satisfy Assumptions 1,2,3, with $||A||_{W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )} \le \sigma ^{-1}$ and $||\gamma _k||_{W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )} \le \sigma ^{-1},\,  k=1,2$. Then there exist constants $C>0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$ depending only on $\Omega $, $d$, $\sigma $, $g_1$ and the coefficients of $L_1$ such that \begin{equation}  \Vert \gamma _2-\gamma _1\Vert _{L^\infty (\Omega _d)} \le C\left(\Vert \gamma _2-\gamma _1\Vert _{L^\infty (\partial \Omega )} +\Vert u_2-u_1\Vert _{W^{2,1}(\Omega )}\right)^\alpha \end{equation} for any $g_2$ and $\gamma _2$ of an admissible pair $(\gamma _1,\,  \gamma _2)$. Furthermore, if $\Omega $ has an analytic smooth boundary and if $g_1$ is analytic in $\partial \Omega $ and all the coefficients of $L_1$ are analytic near $\partial \Omega $, then we have the estimate} (\ref{eq::stability}) {\emph in which $L^\infty (\Omega _d)$ is replaced with $L^\infty (\Omega )$.}\\

Furthermore, if $\Omega $ has an analytic smooth boundary and if $g_1$ is analytic in $\partial \Omega $ and all the coefficients of $L_1$ are analytic near $\partial \Omega $, then we have the estimate} (\ref{eq::stability}) {\emph in which $L^\infty (\Omega _d)$ is replaced with $L^\infty (\Omega )$.}\\

title: TheoremSearch: uniqueness and Lipschitz stability for recovering piecewise constant diffusion coefficient in one-di
text: uniqueness and Lipschitz stability for recovering piecewise constant diffusion coefficient in one-dimensional parabolic equation from interior point measurements For a Lipschitz domain D, given functions a and b in class A1, and a positive bounded function f, the L2 norm of the difference between a and b is bounded by a constant times the H01 norm of the difference between their corresponding solutions raised to the power one-sixth. The constant depends on the domain, dimension, ellipticity parameters, and the lower bound of f. The inequality also involves a constant C0 from a prior definition. This result provides a stability estimate for the inverse problem of recovering coefficients from solutions. There exists exactly one real constant such that a particular equation has a solution. This solution is a Lipschitz continuous function defined on the closure of a domain. The constant is uniquely determined. The solution exists for that specific constant. The problem describes a diffusion equation with a positive, integrable coefficient function. It states that the initial value problem has at most one solution. This uniqueness holds under the condition that the solution is square integrable over space. Under certain smoothness and support conditions on the initial data, and with given functions satisfying continuity and non-vanishing properties, the inverse problem has a unique solution. The coefficient function is continuous on the time interval. The assumptions ensure the associated equation is uniformly parabolic.

text: Cramer-Rao bound attainment maximum likelihood estimator nonlinear least squares Gaussian noise small noise asymptotic efficiency Maximum likelihood estimation achieves the lowest possible variance for parameter estimation when the noise is Gaussian. This optimality is defined by the Cramér-Rao lower bound. The bound represents the smallest achievable variance for an unbiased estimator. For a linear model with complex Gaussian noise, the minimum variance unbiased estimator is given by the least squares solution. The covariance matrix of this estimator equals the inverse Fisher information matrix. This estimator achieves the Cramer-Rao lower bound, indicating it is efficient. The bound is met with equality when the Fisher information matrix is diagonal. Under certain hypotheses, the maximum likelihood estimator is asymptotically efficient. It achieves the lower bound specified by a referenced theorem. This means it attains the smallest possible variance in the limit. The Cramer-Rao lower bound applies to an unbiased estimator of a normalized signal parameter from noisy linear measurements. The noise is Gaussian with independent entries of known variance. The parameter is defined by scaling the signal by the sign of its last nonzero element. The estimator's covariance matrix minus the inverse Fisher information is positive semidefinite for parameters in the interior of the domain.

title: Theorem 5 — Time-Spread Pilot-Based Channel Estimation for Backscatter Networks
text: For a linear model with complex Gaussian noise, the minimum variance unbiased estimator is given by the least squares solution. The covariance matrix of this estimator equals the inverse Fisher information matrix. This estimator achieves the Cramer-Rao lower bound, indicating it is efficient. The bound is met with equality when the Fisher information matrix is diagonal. \cite[Theorem 4.1]{kay1993fundamentals} If the data observed can be modeled as\begin{eqnarray} \label{LinearModel_Kay} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{D}\bm {\theta } + \mathbf{w}, \end{eqnarray}where $\mathbf{y}$ is an $N \times 1$ vector of observations, $\mathbf{D}$ is a known $N \times p$ matrix (with $N>p$) with rank $p$, $\bm {\theta }$ is a $p \times 1$ vector of parameters to be estimated, and $\mathbf{w}$ is an $N \times 1$ noise vector with PDF $\mathcal{CN}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma ^2 \mathbf{I})$, then the MVU estimator is\begin{eqnarray}  \hat{\bm {\theta }} = ( \mathbf{D}^{\rm {H}} \mathbf{D})^{-1} \mathbf{D}^{\rm {H}} \mathbf{y}, \end{eqnarray}And the covariance matrix of $\hat{\bm {\theta }}$ is\begin{eqnarray}  \mathbf{C}_{\hat{\bm {\theta }}} = \sigma ^2 ( \mathbf{D}^{\rm {H}} \mathbf{D})^{-1}. \end{eqnarray}For the linear model \eqref{LinearModel_Kay}, the MVU estimator attains the CRLB. Therefore, we have $\mathbf{C}_{\hat{\bm {\theta }}} = \mathcal{I}^{-1}(\bm {\theta })$, where $\mathcal{I}(\bm {\theta })$ is the Fisher information matrix, satisfying \cite[Theorem 3.2]{kay1993fundamentals}\begin{eqnarray} \label{LowerBound} [\mathbf{C}_{\hat{\bm {\theta }}}]_{i,i} = [ \mathcal{I}^{-1}(\bm {\theta })]_{i,i}\ge \frac{1}{[\mathcal{I}(\bm {\theta })]_{i,i}}. \end{eqnarray}And equality holds when $\mathcal{I}^{-1}(\bm {\theta })$ is diagonal \cite[Ex. 3.12]{kay1993fundamentals}.

If the solution is bounded below by a positive constant on the inner boundary over time, then the difference in solutions on the accessible boundary controls the difference in Robin coefficients. This holds for all coefficients in a neighborhood of a given coefficient. The stability constant depends on the lower bound and the neighborhood size. Under given conditions, the unique solution to the parabolic equation with initial condition linear in x is Lipschitz continuous in both time and space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the slope parameter theta. This constant is given by a function kappa of theta, which is locally bounded. The result holds for all real values of theta. The fundamental solution of a divergence-form parabolic equation with a measurable, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix satisfies a specific derivative estimate. The coefficient matrix is assumed to be Lipschitz continuous in the spatial variable. The constants in the estimate depend only on the ellipticity constant, the dimension, and the Lipschitz constant. For a constant p between 1 and infinity, assume the coefficients a are continuous with specified moduli of continuity on different parts of the domain. For any f in L_p, there exists a unique strong solution u in the Sobolev space W^{1,2}_p to the given parabolic equation with zero Dirichlet boundary condition. The solution satisfies an estimate where its norm is bounded by a constant times the norm of f. The constant depends only on the dimension, p, the ellipticity constant, and the moduli of continuity.

title: TheoremSearch: Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt local convergence for nonlinear least squares parameter estimati
text: Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt local convergence for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with well-conditioned Jacobian and small Gaussian noise, estimator attains Cramer-Rao bound asymptotically Maximum likelihood estimation achieves the lowest possible variance for parameter estimation when the noise is Gaussian. This optimality is defined by the Cramér-Rao lower bound. The bound represents the smallest achievable variance for an unbiased estimator. The Cramer-Rao lower bound applies to an unbiased estimator of a normalized signal parameter from noisy linear measurements. The noise is Gaussian with independent entries of known variance. The parameter is defined by scaling the signal by the sign of its last nonzero element. The estimator's covariance matrix minus the inverse Fisher information is positive semidefinite for parameters in the interior of the domain. For white Gaussian noise with covariance sigma squared times the identity matrix, the Cramer-Rao bound is at least N theta times sigma squared divided by two times the squared two-norm of M. Equality holds if the derivative of h sub M p with respect to theta, conjugated and multiplied by M conjugate transpose M over the squared norm of M and then by the derivative of h sub M p, equals the derivative of h sub M p conjugate transpose multiplied by the derivative of h sub M p. The local minimizer's squared error converges to the minimum mean squared error. Conditional expectations of functions of the true parameter given transformed estimates approach a Gaussian mixture expectation. The transformation parameter converges to a specific value. These results hold under the theorem's conditions.

text: local convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with injective Jacobian and small noise Given a set of parameters and controls satisfying a rank condition, the Gauss-Newton method converges to the true parameters when initialized near them, provided the initial error is sufficiently small. The convergence holds for a specific minimization problem involving linear system outputs. The result depends on the smallest singular value of a constructed matrix. If the matrix derivative of S at nu-hat is injective, then the Gauss-Newton algorithm converges locally. If the derivative is also Lipschitz continuous, then the convergence becomes locally quadratic. Under certain conditions on the function G and its derivative, if the initial guess is close to a solution, then the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm stopped by the discrepancy principle ends after finitely many steps. The resulting approximations converge to a solution as the noise level decreases to zero. The Gauss-Newton method converges to a solution for a nonlinear least squares problem under certain conditions. The method is well-defined and the sequence remains within a ball around the solution. The convergence rate is bounded by an expression involving the initial error and a function f. The radius of convergence is optimal under additional equality conditions, and the solution is unique under a further hypothesis.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Log-space multistart Levenberg–Marquardt MLE through the forward model reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: With 4 parameters, a Fisher condition number of roughly 48 and sigma=0.001, the forward map F: [0.5,2]^4 -> R^{4xT} is locally well-conditioned. Per-sample bounded LM in log k with 3 starts and 30 iterations should converge to the global least-squares minimiser on almost all samples. That would give val rel_l2 close to the CRB floor of about 0.019, and clearly below 0.05. The noise is additive i.i.d. Gaussian and the forward model is exactly known, so the MLE is asymptotically efficient. Its error covariance should approach the inverse Fisher information, and the harness CRB gives rel_l2 of about 0.0186. The log transform makes the positivity constraint implicit. It also roughly equalises the sensitivity scaling, because the diffusive time scale goes like 1/k. Multistart guards against local minima created by the discontinuous coefficient. Learned regressors trained on only 3000 samples are unlikely to reach this efficiency. context.forward is the exact discretised map that generated the data (no model error) The least-squares landscape in log k has a dominant basin, and 3 starts suffice to find it The explicit FD scheme is stable over the whole box (k<=2 with 40 points and 200 steps); the harness generated data with it, so this is assumed Forward-model budget permits about 750 samples x 3 starts x 30 iterations, using Jacobian calls

assumptions: context.forward is the exact discretised map that generated the data (no model error)
The least-squares landscape in log k has a dominant basin, and 3 starts suffice to find it
The explicit FD scheme is stable over the whole box (k<=2 with 40 points and 200 steps); the harness generated data with it, so this is assumed
Forward-model budget permits about 750 samples x 3 starts x 30 iterations, using Jacobian calls
data.falsifiable_test: Run on the val split. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 > 0.035, which is nearly twice the CRB floor and would indicate local minima or model mismatch. It is also falsified if more than 5% of samples have per-sample relative error > 0.2, which would indicate convergence failures.
data.if_fails: A large error concentrated in k1 and k4 means weak boundary-segment sensitivity is the bottleneck, so the prior should be used through MMSE or Tikhonov. Scattered outliers mean multimodality, so a learned initialiser (hybrid) is needed.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Hybrid: learned initialiser plus posterior-mean refinement beats MLE by exploiting the bounded uniform prior on poorly-determined end segments
text: rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, and the prior is a bounded box. Under these conditions the MMSE estimator (posterior mean from importance sampling on the Laplace approximation) has lower expected rel_l2 than the MLE, mainly for k1 and k4. Near the bounds 0.5 and 2.0, MLE clipping and noise inflate error, and the posterior mean shrinks correctly. A ridge or extra-trees initialiser on log features gives a basin-correct start, so only about 15 LM iterations are needed. Predicted val rel_l2 is at least 5% relative lower than the best pure-physics MLE run. For squared loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean. When the CRB std of 2% is non-negligible relative to the distance to the bound, the box truncates the likelihood asymmetrically. The MLE is then biased in the wrong direction, and MMSE corrects this. A learned initialiser on 3000 simulated samples supplies a global basin estimate that does not depend on multistart luck, and it also saves forward-model budget. The posterior is approximately Gaussian in log k, so the Laplace approximation is a good proposal, given high SNR (sigma=0.001) An extra-trees model on log-temperature features is accurate to within the LM basin, roughly 10-20% relative error Gains appear because a non-trivial fraction of the true k values lie within about 2 CRB std of a bound, or because the likelihood is non-quadratic in k1 and k4

assumptions: The posterior is approximately Gaussian in log k, so the Laplace approximation is a good proposal, given high SNR (sigma=0.001)
An extra-trees model on log-temperature features is accurate to within the LM basin, roughly 10-20% relative error
Gains appear because a non-trivial fraction of the true k values lie within about 2 CRB std of a bound, or because the likelihood is non-quadratic in k1 and k4
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 with the physics-MLE arm from proposal 1. The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid posterior-mean result is not at least 5% relatively better, or if the k1 and k4 per-component errors do not decrease. As an ablation, the same hybrid with estimator=mode separates the MMSE effect from the initialiser effect.

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned amortized initializer + few-step log-space Levenberg–Marquardt refinement reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: A torch_mlp trained on the 3000 simulated samples gives estimates inside the Gauss–Newton basin of attraction. A few bounded LM iterations in log-k space through the exact forward model then cut val rel_l2 to at most 0.035, which is within about 2x of the CRB floor of 0.0186. The MLP alone should land around 0.05 to 0.08. The forward map is a finite composition of explicit finite-difference steps, so it is a polynomial and therefore smooth in k, even though k(x) is discontinuous in space. The Fisher matrix is full rank (median condition number 48), and CRB relative std per parameter is at most 2.2%. Under these conditions the local MLE is close to efficient, and the main risk for pure physics is a poor start or a wasted multistart budget. An amortized learned initializer removes most iterations and the risk of local minima. LM then removes the approximation bias of the network, which limits pure regression with 3000 samples. The log transform enforces positivity and makes the sensitivities better balanced across the [0.5, 2] range. The MLP initial error is small enough to be inside the local convergence region of GN/LM. Forward and Jacobian calls for about 750 val + 750 test samples x about 10 iterations fit in the 120 s per-experiment limit. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 1e-3 as stated, so unweighted least squares is the MLE. The explicit scheme is stable for all k in [0.5, 2] (the harness simulator defines this).

Forward and Jacobian calls for about 750 val + 750 test samples x about 10 iterations fit in the 120 s per-experiment limit.
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 1e-3 as stated, so unweighted least squares is the MLE.
The explicit scheme is stable for all k in [0.5, 2] (the harness simulator defines this).
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid with that of its own MLP initializer. The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid val rel_l2 > 0.035, or if the hybrid fails to improve on the initializer by at least 30% relative.
data.if_fails: Hybrid error near the MLP error, with large residuals, means the learned init is outside the basin or LM is not converging; that points to more starts, or Tikhonov damping toward the init. Hybrid error stalling near 0.03-0.05 with residuals at the noise level means MLE is inefficient at the box edges (k1, k4 clipped). The next test is then the posterior_mean estimator, which is the MMSE under the box prior.

author: researcher-ml
title: Pure amortized MLP with noise-matched augmentation and log targets meets the 0.05 threshold without forward-model calls at inference
text: The inverse map from 4 sensor time series to log k is smooth and low-dimensional: the 4 parameters are well-identified with Fisher condition number about 48. An MLP trained on 3000 samples with log targets, standardized raw features and on-the-fly noise augmentation at the true sigma should therefore reach val rel_l2 < 0.05. It should beat kernel_ridge and ridge by at least 40% relative, because the map is nonlinear: sensor responses scale roughly like exp(-k t) in the diffusion time. This tests whether physics refinement is needed at all. If the learned map alone reaches the target, inference is essentially free. It also isolates the representation question: log targets match the multiplicative structure of k in the diffusion time scale. Noise augmentation at sigma = 1e-3 trains the network on the correct noisy feature distribution and acts as a Tikhonov-like regularizer. The 3000 samples cover a 4-D prior box densely (about 7 per axis in a grid-equivalent sense), which is plausibly enough for a smooth map. The inverse map is smooth enough on the prior box that 3000 samples suffice, with no sharp folds from non-identifiability. Training-feature noise matches the val/test noise level (sigma = 1e-3). Early stopping on an internal split prevents overfitting with about 200k parameters.

assumptions: The inverse map is smooth enough on the prior box that 3000 samples suffice, with no sharp folds from non-identifiability.
Training-feature noise matches the val/test noise level (sigma = 1e-3).
Early stopping on an internal split prevents overfitting with about 200k parameters.
data.falsifiable_test: The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 >= 0.05, or if the MLP does not beat the best of ridge and kernel_ridge by at least 40% relative on val.
data.if_fails: An MLP plateau around 0.06-0.10 would show that the 3000-sample approximation error dominates. That would justify the hybrid (proposal 1), or training on additional simulated samples generated through context.forward in a custom_solver. A gap that concentrates on k1 and k4 would confirm that the boundary segments are the bottleneck, pointing to per-parameter loss weighting by inverse CRB variance.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Amortized init + forward-model refinement scored by posterior mean (MMSE), not MLE
text: Per-sample error, not sample size, is what limits this problem. A learned initializer (torch_mlp, log-target) followed by a few log-space Levenberg-Marquardt steps through the exact forward model, then importance-sampled posterior-mean estimation under the box prior, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.03. That is within about 1.6x of the CRB floor of 0.0186. It will also beat both the pure learned map and the MLE ('mode') variant of the same pipeline. The gain over MLE should come mostly from k1 and k4. Most pipelines frame the problem as either 'learn the inverse map' or 'solve MLE per sample'. I question both halves. (a) The CRB relative stds are 0.6% for the interior segments and 2% for the end segments. Reaching that resolution requires the inverse map to be accurate to well under 1%, which is hard to learn from 3000 samples over 800 correlated features. Refining through F(theta) removes that approximation error. (b) The metric is a squared-error-type loss under a known uniform prior. The Bayes-optimal point estimate is the posterior mean, not the MLE. The MLE is only unbiased with CRB-level variance when the Fisher information is non-degenerate and the estimate stays inside the box. For k1 and k4 the information is weak and draws near 0.5 or 2.0 get clipped. In that regime MMSE shrinkage can lower the error, and it may even go below the unbiased CRB, because the CRB constrains unbiased estimators only. Working in log space matches the positivity constraint. The Jacobian of a diffusion forward map is also closer to scale-invariant in log k. The forward model given to the hybrid is the same discretization that generated the data (no model error) Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=0.001, as stated, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is a reasonable importance-sampling proposal The MLP initializer is within the LM basin of attraction for most samples (the Fisher condition number median of 48 suggests mild, not severe, ill-conditioning) rel_l2 is aggregated in a way dominated by squared-type per-sample error, so MMSE is the appropriate Bayes estimator

assumptions: The forward model given to the hybrid is the same discretization that generated the data (no model error)
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=0.001, as stated, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is a reasonable importance-sampling proposal
The MLP initializer is within the LM basin of attraction for most samples (the Fisher condition number median of 48 suggests mild, not severe, ill-conditioning)
rel_l2 is aggregated in a way dominated by squared-type per-sample error, so MMSE is the appropriate Bayes estimator
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 across three settings: (i) the initializer alone, (ii) the hybrid with estimator='mode', (iii) the hybrid with estimator='posterior_mean'. Also report per-parameter relative error. The hypothesis is falsified if any of these hold: (iii) has val rel_l2 >= 0.03; (iii) is not lower than (ii); or the improvement from (ii) to (iii) is not concentrated in k1 and k4.
data.if_fails: If the mode variant is already about 0.02 and posterior_mean does not help, the problem is effectively in the asymptotic, interior regime and MLE is enough. Further effort should then go to cost rather than estimator choice. If even the mode variant is well above the floor, the initializer leaves samples outside the basin, or there is a mismatch between the data generator and context.forward. Either should be checked with residual chi-square diagnostics.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Questioning the fixed-training-set framing: simulation-amplified amortized inference in log-k
text: The 3000-sample training set is an artificial bottleneck. The forward model is available and the noise model is known, so the training set can be enlarged with 6000 extra prior draws simulated through context.forward plus sigma=0.001 Gaussian noise. An MLP trained on the result, in log-k target space, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.045 with no per-sample optimization at prediction time. It will also beat the same MLP trained on the 3000 provided samples alone by at least 20% relative. The task statement presents this as supervised regression with a fixed n, but the constraint only requires training on simulated data, and context.forward is a simulator. This is the simulation-based-inference (neural posterior / amortized estimation) setting rather than the classical fixed-dataset setting. Because the noise is Gaussian and the loss is squared, a regressor trained on prior-distributed simulations converges toward the posterior mean, which is the Bayes-optimal estimator. If the learned-map error is mainly variance from too few samples, tripling n should cut it sharply. This proposal is the direct competitor to proposal 1. It tests whether the forward model is better spent on generating training data or on refining each sample, a question the standard framing never asks. context.forward(theta) returns observations in the same feature ordering and shape as X; the code falls back to the provided data only if the dimensions mismatch The forward-call budget allows about 6000 evaluations The provided training data were generated from the same prior and noise model, so the simulated and provided samples are exchangeable The inverse map is smooth enough in log k for a 2-layer MLP to approximate it to about 3% accuracy

assumptions: context.forward(theta) returns observations in the same feature ordering and shape as X; the code falls back to the provided data only if the dimensions mismatch
The forward-call budget allows about 6000 evaluations
The provided training data were generated from the same prior and noise model, so the simulated and provided samples are exchangeable
The inverse map is smooth enough in log k for a 2-layer MLP to approximate it to about 3% accuracy
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of this solver against an otherwise identical MLP trained only on the 3000 provided samples (n_sim=0 or a dimension mismatch). The hypothesis is falsified if either val rel_l2 >= 0.045 or the relative improvement from simulation amplification is below 20%. Log whether the fallback path was taken, so a mismatch is not mistaken for a null effect.
data.if_fails: If amplification does not help, the learned-map error is approximation or bias rather than variance from small n, and per-sample forward refinement (proposal 1) is the right use of the simulator. If it helps but stalls above 0.045, a natural follow-up combines the two: use this amplified MLP as the hybrid initializer.

text: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with bounds The gradient of f is Lipschitz continuous with constant L. The Hessian approximations are bounded above and below by positive constants. The sequence of parameters produced by the algorithm is bounded. The estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter as the sample size increases. This holds under specific conditions on the parameter bounds and the assumptions of a referenced theorem. The parameter values are constrained within a defined interval. The result applies to a particular estimator defined in a prior equation. The function L is bounded above and below by expressions involving the Frobenius norm of the estimated parameter matrix. The upper bound is a linear function of the squared norm plus a constant. The lower bound is the squared norm itself. The function L is bounded in probability if and only if the parameter estimate is bounded in probability. An estimable parameter is bounded.

author: researcher-experimental
title: TheoremSearch: Matched-noise training augmentation
text: Matched-noise training augmentation Training with noise is equivalent to adding a regularizer to the loss function. The regularizer is a designed function applied to the learning model. The loss function with noise approximates the original loss plus a constant times the regularizer. This relationship holds for the model parameters with and without noise. Given a symmetric sequence of object pairs, if the data augmentation policy equals the distribution derived from the Untied MixUp parameters, then the Untied MixUp loss equals the data augmentation training loss. Given a distribution of labeled examples with standard normal inputs, applying a specific augmentation algorithm produces a new distribution. For any real function and unit vector, the expected value of the function applied to the dot product under the augmented distribution equals the expected value of the noise-operator-transformed function under the original distribution. This holds provided the original expectation is finite. Training with Gaussian noise added to labels increases the output variance compared to training with original labels. The expected mean of the model outputs remains the same in both cases. These results hold after one step of stochastic gradient descent. The theorem compares two training scenarios with and without label noise.

Given an initial model $f_{\theta _0}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb {R}^m$ and a dataset $\{ (x_i, y_i)\} _{i=1}^N$, where $x_i \in \mathcal{X}$ and $y_i \in \mathbb {R}^m$ are inputs and labels. Consider two training scenarios:\begin{enumerate}[label=(0),topsep=0pt,itemsep=2pt]\item Training with the original labels $y_i$. 

\item Training with Gaussian noise perturbed labels $y_i + \varepsilon _i$, where $\varepsilon _i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma ^2 I_m)$. 

\end{enumerate}After one step of SGD, the following properties hold:\begin{enumerate}[label=(),topsep=0pt,itemsep=2pt]\item $\mathcal{V}(f_{\theta _1}^{(2)}) > \mathcal{V}(f_{\theta _1}^{(1)})$: Adding Gaussian noise to the labels increases the variance of the model outputs. 

\item $\mathbb {E}[\bar{f}_{\theta _1}^{(2)}] = \bar{f}_{\theta _1}^{(1)}$: The expectation of the mean of the model outputs remains unchanged. 

\end{enumerate}

Training with Gaussian noise added to labels increases the output variance compared to training with original labels. The expected mean of the model outputs remains the same in both cases. These results hold after one step of stochastic gradient descent. The theorem compares two training scenarios with and without label noise. Consider two training scenarios:\begin{enumerate}[label=(0),topsep=0pt,itemsep=2pt]\item Training with the original labels $y_i$. 

\item Training with Gaussian noise perturbed labels $y_i + \varepsilon _i$, where $\varepsilon _i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma ^2 I_m)$.

\end{enumerate}

text: rel_l2 vs LM iteration (0, 2, 4, 8, 12) starting from the MLP init Under given conditions, the number of LAMM iterations needed to produce a sequence of approximate solutions is on the order of C1 times the inverse square of the initial error tolerance plus C2 times the number of steps minus one multiplied by the logarithm of the inverse of the subsequent error tolerance. The constants C1 and C2 are positive and do not depend on the sample size, dimension, or sparsity. The initial error bound is proportional to a parameter lambda, and later bounds are proportional to the inverse square root of the sample size. Under given assumptions and for a fixed time step size, the iteration is well-defined for all steps starting from any initial guess in the L2 space. The iteration complexity of the algorithm is of order L times the squared distance from the initial point to the optimum, divided by epsilon. This bound holds under the same assumptions as the referenced theorem. The result provides a measure of how many steps are needed to achieve a given accuracy. The maximum number of iterations needed to achieve a relative accuracy of at most delta is bounded above by a constant times L divided by mu, multiplied by the sum of the natural logarithm of four times the initial accuracy and the positive part of the square root of one over delta minus two.

text: Given a sample from the posterior, the distance between the true conditional distribution and a model is bounded by the expected distance between two independent model samples. This holds for any statistical distance convex in its first argument. Similarly, for distances convex in the second argument, the same bound applies with the arguments reversed. These inequalities lead to corresponding bounds in expectation over the joint distribution. Let $W'$ be a sample from the posterior distribution $P_{W|X,Z^n}$, such that $W$ and $W'$ are conditionally i.i.d.\  given $(X,Z^n)$. Then for any $(w,x,z^n)$ and any statistical distance $D$ that is convex in the first argument,\begin{align}  D(P_{Y|x,z^n} , K_{Y|x,w}) \le \mathbf{E}[D(K_{Y|x,W'} , K_{Y|x,w})|x,z^n] , \end{align}and consequently,\begin{align}  \mathbf{E}[ D(P_{Y|X,Z^n} , K_{Y|X,W}) ] \le \mathbf{E}[ D(K_{Y|X,W'} , K_{Y|X,W}) ] \end{align}where the expectations are taken with respect to the joint distribution of $(W,X,Z^n,W')$. Similarly, for any $(w,x,z^n)$ and any statistical distance $D$ that is convex in the second argument,\begin{align}  D(K_{Y|x,w} , P_{Y|x,z^n}) \le \mathbf{E}[D(K_{Y|x,w} , K_{Y|x,W'} ) | x,z^n] , \end{align}and consequently,\begin{align}  \mathbf{E}[ D(K_{Y|X,W}, P_{Y|X,Z^n} ) ] \le \mathbf{E}[ D( K_{Y|X,W} , K_{Y|X,W'} ) ] . \end{align}

title: Reference arm: log-space multistart LM MLE is statistically efficient (at the CRB floor) with a verified forward model
text: With a verified exact forward model and i.i.d. Gaussian noise of known sigma, the log-k LM MLE (3 starts, 30 iterations) is efficient on the full validation split. Three outcomes are predicted. First, val rel_l2 / CRB floor <= 1.15, so rel_l2 <= about 0.0215. Second, fewer than 1% of samples have per-sample relative error > 0.2. Third, the mean chi^2/dof lies in [0.9, 1.05]. The 60-sample pilot gave rel_l2 = 0.0190 against a CRB floor of 0.0186. It gave chi^2/dof = 0.944 and residual std at the truth of 0.000995 against sigma = 0.001. Gauss-Newton z_rms was 0.98. All three are what an efficient, correctly specified MLE should produce. The full run is needed to confirm efficiency with a CI, and it then becomes the reference that every hybrid and data-driven arm is compared against on identical samples. context.forward is the data-generating map. Tested: residual std at truth 0.000995 vs 0.001; no mismatch flagged on 200 samples. The log-k least-squares landscape has one dominant basin. Partially tested: rel_l2 is at the CRB floor and calibration is good. To be confirmed by the start-agreement rate. Aggregation of rel_l2 is comparable to the harness CRB-floor estimate. Untested, so the ratio criterion is used with that caveat. The forward-call budget suffices: about 15k evaluations for 60 samples, so about 190k for 750, which is cheap per call.

data.falsifiable_test: The test runs on the full validation split (750 samples) with a bootstrap 95% CI. The hypothesis is falsified if any of four conditions holds: (a) the CI lower bound on rel_l2 exceeds 1.15 × 0.01856 = 0.0213; (b) more than 1% of samples have per-sample relative error > 0.2, indicating basin failure; (c) mean chi^2/dof falls outside [0.9, 1.05], indicating mismatch or non-convergence; (d) the start-disagreement rate (starts converging to MLEs differing by more than 3 GN-std) exceeds 5%. Boundary bias is reported separately: per-component MSE stratified by whether the true k_i is within 2 CRB std of 0.5 or 2.0.
data.if_fails: If (a) fails but (b) to (d) pass, the CRB floor estimate (32 draws) or the aggregation is mismatched, not the estimator. If (b) or (d) fails, the landscape is multimodal and the hybrid initialisers become essential. If (c) fails, the forward model or noise convention is wrong, and all physics and hybrid arms must be reinterpreted.

title: Initializer ablation: cheap extra-trees (raw features) + 15-iteration LM reaches the MLE accuracy at fewer total LM iterations than 3-start MLE
text: An extra-trees initializer on raw features lands in the MLE basin for at least 99% of validation samples. If so, 15 LM iterations with 1 extra start give rel_l2 statistically indistinguishable from P-001 (a paired bootstrap CI on the difference that contains 0, with |Δ| < 0.001). This uses half the per-sample LM iterations (2 × 15 vs 3 × 30). The extra-trees initializer alone gives rel_l2 in [0.05, 0.15], which is a basin-quality start but not a solution. If the landscape has one dominant basin (supported by P-001's pilot), estimator accuracy is fixed by the likelihood, and the initializer only affects cost and robustness. Establishing that a cheap tree initializer suffices bounds the value of more expensive neural initializers (P-003 and P-007). The pilot showed 0.0188 for this hybrid against 0.0190 for the MLE. Raw-feature extra-trees with log targets is within the LM basin (10-20% error). To be tested by initializer-only rel_l2. title: Lemma 7 (cf. Lemma 1 from \cite {rahimi2008weighted}) — Stochastic Nonlinear Control via Finite-dimensional Spectral Dynamic Embedding
text: The true function f star is an integral of a bounded function over a distribution. An estimate f hat is formed by averaging samples from that distribution. The L2 error between the estimate and the true function is bounded with high probability. The bound decreases with the square root of the number of samples.  Let $p$ be a distribution on a space $\Omega $, and consider a mapping $\phi (x;\omega ) \in \mathbb {R}^\ell $. Suppose $$f^*(x) = \int _{\Omega } p(\omega ) \beta (\omega )^\top \phi (x;\omega ) d\omega ,$$ for some vector $\beta (\omega ) \in \mathbb {R}^\ell $ where $\sup _{x,\omega } \left |\beta (\omega )^\top \phi (x;\omega )\right | \leq C$ for some $C > 0$. Consider $\{\omega _i\}_{i=1}^k$ drawn iid from $p$, and denote the sample average of $f^*$ as $\hat {f}(x) = \frac {1}{K} \sum _{k=1}^K \beta (\omega _k)^\top \phi (x;\omega _k)$. Then, for any $\delta > 0$, with probability at least $1 - \delta $ over the random draws of $\{\omega _i\}_{i=1}^k$, $$\sqrt {\int _{\mathcal {X}} \left (\hat {f}(x) - f^*(x)\right )^2 d\mu (x)} \leq \frac {C}{\sqrt {K}}\left ( 1 + \sqrt {2\log \frac {1}{\delta }}\right ).$$

title: TheoremSearch: Bayesian Cramer-Rao (van Trees) bound with uniform prior on a bounded interval
text: Bayesian Cramer-Rao (van Trees) bound with uniform prior on a bounded interval The Bayesian Cramer-Rao bound for the parameter vector m exists under given growth assumptions. It satisfies the information inequality. The Bayesian Cramér-Rao bound provides a lower bound on the mean squared error of any estimator. The bound depends on the prior distribution and the conditional distribution of the data. It is expressed in terms of two information quantities: the Bayesian information and the conditional Bayesian information. The inequality holds for any estimator of the parameter. The Cramér-Rao bound for the minimum mean squared error is given under a binomial observation model. The lower bound depends on the expectation of the inverse of a function involving the variable and its complement. It also includes the expected value of the square of the score function. The bound holds when a specific assumption is satisfied. The universal Cramér-Rao bound applies when using the function phi of u equals u log u. It assumes Y is a Poisson distribution with parameter a times X and that a specific density condition holds. The bound states that the phi-risk of X given Y is at least the reciprocal of D sub c comma c. The constant c is defined by a limit supremum condition.

title: TheoremSearch: input noise injection equivalent to Tikhonov regularization small noise squared loss
text: input noise injection equivalent to Tikhonov regularization small noise squared loss The expected value of the loss function over noise equals the original loss plus a regularization term. This regularization term is defined as the expected difference between the perturbed and true log-partition functions. It approximates to half the sum of the second derivatives of the log-partition function times the variance of the perturbed linear predictors. This result connects noise injection to explicit regularization in the loss function. The expected value of the squared error over noise equals the sum of the squared error without noise and a regularization term. The regularization term is proportional to the squared L2 norm of the parameter vector. The noise is additive and applied to the function output. The equivalence holds for any given prompt consisting of input-output pairs. Adding Gaussian noise to inputs during neural network training with quadratic loss approximates minimizing the expected squared error plus a regularization term. This regularization term is proportional to the squared norm of the function's gradient. The equivalence holds up to higher order terms. This approach effectively penalizes large gradients, encouraging smoother model outputs. Training with noise is equivalent to adding a regularizer to the loss function. The regularizer is a designed function applied to the learning model. The loss function with noise approximates the original loss plus a constant times the regularizer. This relationship holds for the model parameters with and without noise.

results.body: Given any prompt $P_{\boldsymbol {\lambda }}\coloneqq ({\boldsymbol v}_1,y_1,\cdots ,{\boldsymbol v}_N,y_N)$, we have the following equivalence:\begin{equation}  \mathbb {E}_{\boldsymbol {\epsilon }}\left[\frac{1}{2N}\sum _{i=1}^N(y_i-\boldsymbol {\lambda }^\top \left(f({\boldsymbol v}_i)+\boldsymbol {\epsilon }_i\right))^2\right]=\frac{1}{2N}\sum _{i=1}^N(y_i-\boldsymbol {\lambda }^\top f({\boldsymbol v}_i))^2+\frac{\tau }{2}\left\|  \boldsymbol {\lambda } \right\| _2^2. \end{equation}

results.slogan: Adding Gaussian noise to inputs during neural network training with quadratic loss approximates minimizing the expected squared error plus a regularization term. This regularization term is proportional to the squared norm of the function's gradient. The equivalence holds up to higher order terms. This approach effectively penalizes large gradients, encouraging smoother model outputs.
results.body: \citep {bishop1995training} Training a feed-forward neural-network model using the quadratic (or mean-squared error) loss, with added Gaussian noise of mean 0 and variance $\sigma ^2$ to the inputs, is equivalent to training with \begin {equation} \label {Noise_Tychonoff} \mathbb E _x\left [\|f(x) - y\|^2 + \sigma ^2 \| \nabla f(x)\|^2 \right ] \end {equation} up to higher order terms.
notes: method-level result: applies if its algorithmic assumptions (e.g. full-rank Jacobian, well-specified noise model) hold — check numerically

results.slogan: Training with noise is equivalent to adding a regularizer to the loss function. The regularizer is a designed function applied to the learning model. The loss function with noise approximates the original loss plus a constant times the regularizer. This relationship holds for the model parameters with and without noise.
results.body: Training with noise is equal to adding a regularizer $\Omega ({{\bf {w}}})$, which can be expressed as\begin{equation}  F(\tilde{{\bf {w}}}) \approx F({\bf {w}}) + \lambda \Omega ({{\bf {w}}}),\\[2mm] \end{equation}where $F(\cdot )$ denotes the loss function, $\Omega (\cdot )$ is the designed function, ${\bf {w}}$ is the learning model, $\tilde{{\bf {w}}}$ represents the learning model including noise, and $\lambda $ is a constant.
notes: method-level result: applies if its algorithmic assumptions (e.g. full-rank Jacobian, well-specified noise model) hold — check numerically

author: literature
title: Lemma 1 (\textbf {Penalized likelihood in GLMs with whiteout}) — Whiteout: Gaussian Adaptive Noise Regularization in Deep Neural Networks
text: The expected value of the loss function over noise equals the original loss plus a regularization term. This regularization term is defined as the expected difference between the perturbed and true log-partition functions. It approximates to half the sum of the second derivatives of the log-partition function times the variance of the perturbed linear predictors. This result connects noise injection to explicit regularization in the loss function. The expectation of Eqn (\ref {eqn:mle.p}) over the distribution of noise is \begin {align} &\mbox {E}_{\mathbf{e} }(\textstyle \sum _{i=1}^{n}l_p(\mathbf{w} |\tilde {\mathbf{x} }_i,y_i))\!=\!\textstyle \sum _{i=1}^{n}\!l(\mathbf{w} |\mathbf{x} _i,y_i)\!+\!\frac {R(\mathbf{w} )}{d(\tau )},\!\label {eqn:regloss}\\ &\mbox {where } R(\mathbf{w} )\triangleq \textstyle \sum _{i=1}^{n}\mbox {E}_{\mathbf{e} }(A(\tilde {\mathbf{x} }_i\mathbf{w} ))-A(\boldsymbol {\eta }_i)\notag \\ &\qquad \qquad \quad \approx \textstyle \frac {1}{2} \sum _{i=1}^{n}A''(\boldsymbol {\eta }_i)\mbox {Var}(\tilde {\mathbf{x} }_i\mathbf{w} ).\notag \end {align}

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Initializer ablation: an extra-trees start plus a single 15-iteration LM run matches the 3-start MLE at about 1/6 of the forward-call cost
text: An extra-trees initializer (raw features, log targets, trained on the 3000 train samples) puts at least 99% of val samples in the MLE basin. With estimator = mode, 15 LM iterations and no extra starts, the paired rel_l2 difference against P-009 then has a 95% CI inside [-0.001, +0.001]. The forward-call count is at most 0.35× that of P-009. If the landscape is single-basin, the MLE accuracy is fixed by the likelihood, and the initializer only buys cost and robustness. The arm is now a clean contrast with P-009: same estimator, same transform, same Tikhonov. Only the start strategy and the iteration budget differ. With 3000 training samples, the initializer's relative error is about 2–15%, which is within the LM basin. LM converges quadratically within 15 iterations from a basin start at sigma = 1e-3. The hybrid pipeline reports per-arm forward-call counts. Initializer-only rel_l2 may not be logged.

Following the critic's revision direction, I also drop to extra_starts = 0. The contrast is then 1 × 15 LM iterations against 3 × 30, about a 6× saving if the initializer alone lands in the basin.

author: researcher-ml
title: Missing control: single-start LM MLE from the prior centre (no initializer, no multistart)
text: With a Fisher condition number of about 48 and a log-parameterised, 4-dimensional, box-bounded least-squares problem, the misfit landscape has a single basin over essentially the whole prior box. A single LM run from the prior centre (log-k = log(1.0) area) should therefore reach the same accuracy as the 3-start MLE (P-009) and the learned-initializer hybrids (P-010, P-015). Specifically: val rel_l2 within 3% (relative) of P-009, and below 0.025 in absolute terms. Under this hypothesis, learned initializers and multistart affect cost only (iterations to converge), not accuracy. The critic lists 'an LM run from the prior-mean start (no initializer)' as a missing control. Without it, no initializer or multistart ablation in this round (P-010, P-015, P-017) can tell whether initialization matters for accuracy at all. It is the cheapest physics arm: one start instead of three, so roughly one third of P-009's LM cost. It therefore fits inside the remaining budget headroom the critic identified. From the ML side, this sets the bar a learned inverse map must clear: if the cold-start MLE already sits at the CRB, amortized maps can only win on wall-clock cost, never on rel_l2. The harness starts multistart=1 at the prior centre (or the transformed-space centre) rather than at a random draw. If it starts at a random draw, the test becomes 'single random start', which is a slightly weaker but still informative control. 30 LM iterations are enough to converge from the centre. The worst case is samples with k near 0.5 or 2.0, which are at most about 0.7 in log-distance from the centre. The forward model passed to LM matches the data generator, as the P-009 pilot reported by reaching the CRB floor. Noise is Gaussian with sigma = 0.001, so least squares is the correct likelihood.

data.falsifiable_test: Pair this arm with P-009 on the 750 val samples. Falsified if either of the following holds: (a) val rel_l2 exceeds 1.03 times P-009's value; or (b) more than 1% of samples have per-sample relative error above 3 times their P-009 error, which would indicate local-minimum or non-convergence failures. Also report the per-sample error quantiles (50/90/99) and the fraction of samples that hit the iteration cap.
data.if_fails: If single start is clearly worse than 3-start, multimodality or slow convergence near the bounds is real. Initializers then matter for accuracy, which justifies P-010, P-015 and P-017 on accuracy grounds and not only on cost. The failing samples should be concentrated at extreme k1 and k4 values; that concentration would locate where an amortized initializer earns its keep. If single start matches 3-start, all initializer research should be reframed as cost reduction only.

title: GCV-ridge linear-inverse baseline (raw features, log target): how much of the inverse map is linear?
text: H1: the inverse map from raw sensor time series to log k is materially nonlinear over [0.5,2]^4, so GCV-tuned ridge gives val rel_l2 > 0.06, at least 1.8x the pilot MLP (0.0325) and more than 3x the CRB floor. Falsified if ridge reaches ≤ 0.05, or if its paired-bootstrap CI against the best learned arm in this round overlaps. This is the required missing control. It quantifies the linear share of the inverse and calibrates the value of nonlinear learners and initializers, with regularisation chosen automatically so that a poor score cannot be blamed on mis-set alpha. alpha selected by RidgeCV GCV on the train split only, from a log grid of 1e-4 to 1e3; val is used only for reporting log target via TransformedTargetRegressor; predictions are exponentiated and then clipped by the harness, if it clips standard scaling of raw features; feature count logged noise in the features is matched to val (sigma=1e-3)

author: researcher-experimental
title: Log-feature GCV-ridge: does log(u) linearise the inverse, or does it amplify noise at low-signal sensor times? (single-factor contrast vs P-014)
text: There are two competing mechanisms. H_lin: log temperature approximately linearises the dependence on log k (heat-kernel decay ~ exp(-c·k·t)), so log-feature ridge beats raw-feature ridge (P-014) by ≥ 20% rel_l2. H_noise: entries where u is comparable to sigma=1e-3 (outer sensors at grid indices 5 and 35, early times, far from the central pulse) are noise-amplified by the log, roughly as sigma/u, so log-feature ridge is worse than raw. I predict H_noise dominates and that log-feature ridge stays above 0.06. The discriminating signature is per-parameter: H_noise predicts the k1/k4 errors (outer segments) degrade most, while H_lin predicts uniform improvement. This tests the critic's counterexample to P-014 directly and probes measurement design: which sensor-time entries carry usable signal relative to sigma. The result informs feature design for every learned arm, since raw is used throughout. the harness 'log' feature set applies log to clipped-positive temperatures; the true solution is positive (Gaussian initial condition, homogeneous Dirichlet ends), but noisy readings near 0 can be ≤ 0 everything else identical to revised P-014: RidgeCV GCV grid, standard scaler, log target, same split signal at the outer sensors is near the noise level for part of the window (to be checked: report the fraction of training feature entries with |u| < 5·sigma)

everything else identical to revised P-014: RidgeCV GCV grid, standard scaler, log target, same split
signal at the outer sensors is near the noise level for part of the window (to be checked: report the fraction of training feature entries with |u| < 5·sigma)
data.falsifiable_test: Run a paired bootstrap (2000 resamples, 750 val samples) of per-sample rel_l2 for this arm minus P-014, overall and per parameter. H_lin is supported if the CI lies below 0 and the overall reduction is ≥ 20%. H_noise is supported if the CI lies above 0 and the per-parameter degradation of k1/k4 exceeds that of k2/k3. Report the fraction of training entries with |u| < 5·sigma as the measurement-SNR diagnostic. A null (CI contains 0) means the feature transform is not a lever for linear inverses.
data.if_fails: If log features beat raw by ≥ 20% (H_lin), the learned arms should switch to log features, and P-015/P-016 may be under-using a linearising transform. If neither mechanism shows, sensor SNR is not what limits the linear inverse and the error is purely approximation.

title: Simulation-amplified amortized log-k regression: n_sim 0 vs 6000 at a fixed Adam step count (shared code with P-017)
text: With the full 3000 training samples and a fixed budget of 6000 Adam steps, adding 6000 prior-drawn noisy simulations gives val rel_l2 < 0.033 with no per-sample optimization. This is at least 20% lower than the identical code with n_sim=0, and the paired bootstrap CI on the difference excludes 0. align_z (median chi^2/N of F(y_train) vs X_train) lies in [0.7, 1.5]. A fixed training set is an artificial constraint when an exact simulator is available. This is the cleanest test of whether simulated data reduce amortized error once optimizer steps are equalized. It feeds P-017: if simulations help a lot but the result stays well above 0.019, the remaining gap is approximation error that per-sample likelihood refinement should close. context.forward returns clean observations in the same ordering as X. align_z checks this, and simulation is skipped if align_z >= 3. The 6000 fit-time forward evaluations are within budget (the pilot confirmed this). The train/val data come from the same uniform prior and sigma=0.001 Gaussian noise. At equal step counts, early-stopping-free Adam is not badly overfit at n=3000. If it is, that is part of the measured simulation benefit and is reported as such.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: How many likelihood steps does an amortized estimate need? Simulation-amplified MLP + 0/1/3 box-projected Gauss-Newton steps with monotone acceptance
text: Starting from the P-016 MLP (n_sim=6000, fixed 6000 steps), 3 box-projected, Marquardt-damped log-space Gauss-Newton steps with per-sample monotone acceptance give val rel_l2 < 0.0200. A single step gives rel_l2 within 10% of the 3-step result. Per-parameter relative RMSE falls for all four of k1-k4 from gn_iters=0 to 3. For k1 and k4, the 3-step relative RMSE is at most 1.2x the harness CRB rel std (0.0223 and 0.0179). Physics MLE is already at the floor, so the open question is cost: can an amortized estimate plus one or three cheap likelihood steps (about 6 forward calls per sample per step) replace multistart LM-30? The 0/1/3 design measures the full step-count curve on one shared MLP. A cross-tradition point: amortized SBI provides the basin, and a classical Gauss-Newton step from inside a basin converges quadratically. At SNR this high, one step from a 3% start should take the error below the 0.6% interior resolution. context.forward accepts batched (n,4) arrays in X's ordering; the code falls back to the MLP output on any error. The forward budget covers about 6010 fit evaluations plus (1+5*gn_iters) per sample at prediction, about 12k per 750-sample split at gn_iters=3. Forward differences with h=1e-4 in log-k are accurate: truncation and roundoff errors are both far below sigma=0.001. The MLP estimate lies in the MLE basin for most samples. The n_accept count and the final chi^2/N distribution check this; under the model that distribution should be about 1. Van Trees-type Bayesian bounds (ts:thm:24839008) are not used as the reference, because the uniform box prior has no finite prior Fisher information. The frequentist CRB on the interior is the benchmark.

title: critique r3 of Log-feature GCV-ridge: does log(u) linearise the inverse, or does it amplify noise at low-signal sensor times? (single-f
text: The clipping value for noisy readings ≤0 decides the outcome. Clipping at 1e-8 maps those entries to log ≈ −18. After standard scaling, a handful of such entries per column dominate. The resulting H_noise outcome would be a clipping artefact rather than evidence about sensor SNR. The H_lin mechanism is shaky. At late times, log u ≈ −λ1(k)·t + c, which is linear in λ1, and λ1 is a nonlinear (harmonic-type) function of k, not linear in log k. Early and mid times are mode mixtures. So log features need not linearise a log-k target even in the noiseless case. The headline prediction (>0.06) holds under both H_lin (if the gain is <20% of a large baseline) and H_noise. The discriminating prediction is the sign and size of the paired difference. Make that the registered prediction. Report the fraction of entries with |u| < 5σ BEFORE running. If it is under 1%, H_noise is implausible a priori. Use a noise-aware transform: inside the model, set features=raw, scaler=none and apply a pipeline of FunctionTransformer(arcsinh(X/(2σ))) followed by StandardScaler and then RidgeCV. This is log-like for u≫σ and linear near 0, which separates linearisation from clipping. the physics floor (CRB rel_l2 ~0.01856) is known: what error do you expect relative to it, and what limits a learned inverse here (samples, capacity, noise)? What clip floor does the harness 'log' feature set use? With uniform k, the late-time sensor reading u ≈ A·exp(−π² k t). Then log u is linear in k, so a ridge regression of log k on log u is still nonlinear, and H_lin's linearisation argument fails for the log-k target. Replace the harness log features with the asinh variant (or run both if budget allows: ridge costs <5 s per arm). Test both target parameterisations (log k and k) to address the counterexample.
